hints: After sorting, an optimal matching can use pairs of adjacent remaining values.
A smallest adjacent gap can be selected, but later choices may need to undo that pairing.
Replace its two neighboring gaps by their sum minus the chosen gap, and use a min-heap.
analogy: Think of picking the cheapest link in a chain; a replacement link records the cost of swapping that choice for the two links beside it.
example: Sorted 1,2,3,3,4,7,7,9 gives optimal costs 0, 0, 1, 6 for one through four pairs.
algorithm: Sort the values and put all adjacent gaps in a min-heap and a doubly linked list. Repeatedly take the smallest live gap, add its value to the running answer, and remove it and its immediate neighbors. If both neighbors exist, insert a replacement gap of left + right - chosen between the remaining neighbors; otherwise insert no replacement. Output the running answer after each selection, up to floor(n/2). Use lazy deletion in the heap.
correctness: An uncrossing argument gives an optimal matching on adjacent sorted values. Choosing the minimum gap is safe for one more pair: if a later optimum instead uses both neighboring gaps, the replacement records exactly the extra cost of swapping the chosen gap for those two. Repeating maintains the optimum for each cardinality.
complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
